question.text:
CASE STUDY (continued): The "Sunrise Equity Growth Fund" has an AUM of Rs. 740 crore and charges a TER of 2.10% per annum. Mr. Rajesh holds 10,000 units, and the scheme's current NAV is Rs. 9.87.
Question 4 of 4: What is the approximate annual expense amount borne by Mr. Rajesh's holding due to TER, and how does TER impact his investment returns?

answer.text: Approximately Rs. 2,073 per year; TER reduces the NAV growth, so if the scheme earns 15% gross return, Mr. Rajesh gets approximately 12.90% net return
Approximately Rs. 20,727 per year; TER is charged separately to Mr. Rajesh's bank account
Approximately Rs. 207 per year; TER has minimal impact on long-term returns
Approximately Rs. 2,073 per year; TER has no impact on returns since it is charged to the scheme, not the investor

explanation.text: The Logic: Mr. Rajesh's current holding value = 10,000 x Rs. 9.87 = Rs. 98,700. Annual TER cost on his holding = Rs. 98,700 x 2.10% = Rs. 2,072.70, approximately Rs. 2,073. Per the NISM Series V-A workbook (p.142, p.294), TER is deducted from scheme assets daily and embedded in the NAV — so if the scheme's gross return is 15%, the investor's approximate net return is 15% - 2.10% = approximately 12.90%. The Trap: Rs. 20,727 uses 21% instead of 2.10% (decimal error). TER is not charged separately to the investor's bank account — it is netted off NAV daily. Rs. 207 uses 0.21% (another decimal error). The last option calculates the correct rupee figure but wrongly claims TER has "no impact on returns" — TER directly compresses the net return earned by the investor. Note: Even a Rs. 2,073/year TER cost compounds materially over a long horizon. Use projections with and without TER to help clients see the gap, and choose schemes with a competitive TER within the same category, given the long-run drag costs impose on returns.
